title: Below the Crack
passages:
Ilka seized the limp rope and felt the claimed hand curl around her wrist. One jerk sent her spiraling upward, boots scraping the smooth wall as she tumbled onto a low stone floor behind the source‑room ledger. Ákos and Márk stood, inhaling dry air, their chests steady. Sára remained by the main ledger, her dead hand fused to the page, but her index finger had pulled free enough to point at the wall‑door seam; a grey smudge marked the stone where the nail dragged, and a hairline crack now ran from floor to ceiling, warm to the touch. Ákos pressed his palm to the grain, and the stone shifted, dust falling like snow.  

Ilka lifted the second ledger, five names gleaming. The fifth—Keres—was still wet and unreadable. Whispering Keres aloud, a black drop surged, merged with the ceiling, and a great void yawned open. The disc beneath the step hummed louder, grinding stone as the crack widened into a spiral shaft. The rope tightened, the claimed hand coiling at Ilka’s shoulder, ready to pull.  

They descended the new shaft, past the warm stone, into a vaulted chamber lit by pale light. Shelves held parchment, and a shallow pool reflected the dim glow. Sára’s dead hand pulsed faintly, as if awaiting a name. Ákos placed his palm on the crack, and the ground sighed, letting a thin stream of water escape. The toll stayed at 109, but the disc’s vibration steadied, and the path ahead grew clearer.

The thin stream fell from the crack, struck the pool, and the black drop resting there went still. The silver surface rippled once, then held the ripple, and beyond the pool’s grey reflection a shore came up out of the dark: water, mud, a few broken posts, and a lone figure in a sailor’s coat standing in a weathered boat that creaked without wind. The boat waited. Ilka felt the second ledger press hard against her ribs, its leather warm, and the fifth name burn behind her eyes though she could not hold it. She whispered, “Keres.” The figure in the boat did not turn. Ákos came to her then, palm dusty from the warm stone, and Márk stood behind him, breath eased by the dry air. Sára’s dead hand pulsed against the ledger, and the claimed hand on Ilka’s shoulder drew its rope tight, the frayed end brushing her collar.

Ilka looked at the figure on the water. She thought of the second ledger, of names owed, of ink that spent memory. She thought of the claimed hand, which paid without cost and still waited in the dark. The ripple held, showing the boat, the coat, the empty tiller. Ilka made her decision. She would not go down into the deeper dark. She would follow the ripple to the coast.

She took the second ledger from her shoulder and tucked it into her coat. Ákos began to say her name, but she put a hand up, not angry, just tired. Márk stepped closer, his dry breath slow. Behind them, Sára’s dead finger shifted at the seam, and the pool’s silver light trembled. The claimed hand drew once on the rope, gentle, and its frayed end pulled tighter; Ilka did not look back. She turned from the pool with the second ledger against her side and walked on, following the ripple’s direction.
